messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 39
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Construction Worker
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement, Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Inadequacy: I am inadequate

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Dwayne is a 39-year-old divorced construction worker of mixed North American heritage who presented for an initial psychological assessment reporting a PCL-5 score of 73, indicating severe posttraumatic stress. He was referred following a workplace incident approximately fourteen months ago in which he witnessed a colleague fall from scaffolding three stories above the ground. Dwayne had been working directly below when the man came down, and he reached him first. What he saw in those minutes before the ambulance arrived — the specific colour of the blood pooling on the concrete, the smell of dust and copper that hung in the still air, the involuntary taste of bile that rose in his own throat as he knelt beside his colleague — lodged themselves in his nervous system in ways he could not have anticipated. His colleague survived but with catastrophic injuries, and Dwayne returned to work the following week believing that getting back on site was the right thing to do.

It was not. Over the weeks that followed, the memories returned not as narrative recollections but as vivid sensory fragments — pictures that arrived without invitation, sudden and total: the angle of a limb, the shadow of the scaffold against the sky. More disorienting still was the way smell and taste had become encoded alongside those images. The sharp mineral scent of freshly poured concrete, which surrounded Dwayne every working day, could without warning carry him back to the moment he knelt on that ground. On one occasion, a mouthful of coffee in the site break room produced the same acrid taste he had experienced that afternoon, and he found himself gripping the edge of the table, momentarily unable to locate himself in the present. These sensory memories, arriving unbidden in the environment where he spent most of his waking hours, began to reshape what he understood about himself and the world. He had come to believe that his beliefs about how things worked — that effort and caution could keep a man safe, that competence mattered — had been entirely destroyed by what he had witnessed. Worse, the vividness and uncontrollability of the memories reinforced a deepening conviction that he was fundamentally inadequate: a man who could not protect a colleague, could not manage his own mind, and could not stop bad things from happening no matter what he did.

It was this cluster of appraisals — the helplessness, the inadequacy, the sense that the world had been revealed as arbitrary and indifferent — that drove Dwayne toward the coping strategies he now relied upon. He began gambling on weekday evenings at a casino forty minutes from his apartment, initially telling himself it was a way to unwind. In truth, the noise and controlled risk of the casino floor offered the only reliable interruption to the intrusive images; the excitement of a hand of cards was one of the few states that temporarily displaced the sensory memories. He also began, with some deliberateness, to dissociate — to practise a kind of mental departure from his own body when the images came, blanking out, as he described it, going somewhere else inside himself. And he suppressed his anger with a rigidity that had become a point of private discipline: he never allowed himself to feel or express it, certain that if he permitted any emotion to surface, the rest would follow and he would not be able to contain it. These strategies, born directly from his conviction that he was powerless and broken, in turn kept the traumatic material from being processed. The memories remained raw and unintegrated, and each time they returned with their full sensory force — the smell, the images, the taste — they confirmed again that he was a man who could not control his own inner life, deepening the appraisals of inadequacy and helplessness that had generated the avoidance in the first place.

Over time, the consequences accumulated in concrete ways. He had been passed over for a crew foreman position he had been informally promised, his supervisor citing a change in his reliability and focus. His divorce, finalised two years earlier, had left him living alone, and the gambling had quietly eroded what savings remained. It was the foreman decision — the occupational loss that made the inadequacy feel externally confirmed — that finally brought him to seek help. What he most feared, he said in the intake session, was that what he had seen on that site had shown him something true about himself and the world that could not be undone. What he most hoped, though he said it quietly and without much conviction, was that someone might tell him otherwise.
